paragraphs: 3DOT changes the appearance of a 3D Gaussian Splatting object using a single reference image. The challenge is to preserve the reference texture while making the edited object look coherent from different viewpoints. Editing individual views can produce inconsistencies, while describing the desired change through text can lose distinctive texture characteristics.

The method combines three ways of guiding generation. First, it transfers the reference texture into an initial view and progressively spreads that change to neighboring views. Second, it uses feature differences between consistent and inconsistent outputs to reinforce agreement across viewpoints. Third, it learns a text token describing how the original texture differs from the reference, then uses that token to guide texture preservation.

These components address related but distinct requirements: transferring the intended appearance and keeping that appearance coherent around the object. The reported qualitative and quantitative evaluations support the effectiveness of their combination. The contribution is a coordinated procedure for image-driven texture transfer that preserves texture characteristics while maintaining structural coherence across views.
neurips-2025-3dot-texture-transfer-for-3.tldr: 3DOT transfers texture from one image onto a 3D Gaussian Splatting object through progressive generation and guidance for texture fidelity and view consistency.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a second-moment matrix while protecting the privacy of individual data points. Such a matrix summarizes how the magnitudes and directions of data vary together. The goal is to preserve its spectral structure, meaning its behavior along different directions, even for difficult inputs that satisfy a specified sampling condition.

That condition is subsamplability: a sufficiently large random subset must preserve the original matrix's spectral structure within a chosen multiplicative tolerance, with a specified probability. Building on this assumption, the authors develop a recursive estimation framework satisfying zero-concentrated differential privacy. They establish high-probability accuracy within an arbitrary multiplicative tolerance, expressed as one plus or minus gamma.

The result therefore connects private estimation to a concrete structural property of the data rather than claiming accuracy for every unrestricted input. The authors also show how to apply the algorithm to a distribution's second-moment matrix when a noticeable fraction of observations are outliers. Together, these results provide a route to private matrix estimation with both multiplicative accuracy and outlier tolerance under the stated framework.
neurips-2025-a-private-approximation-of-.tldr: A recursive private estimator preserves second-moment structure with high probability under a subsamplability assumption, with an application to data containing outliers.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner choose which examples to have labeled, while passive learning receives labeled examples without that choice. This paper asks whether selective querying helps in the agnostic setting, where even the best predictor in the chosen class can make errors. It gives a sharp characterization of optimal first-order label-query complexity for every concept class.

The authors also propose a general algorithm that achieves this characterization. Its leading query-complexity term is strictly smaller than the sample complexity of passive supervised learning, with the improvement tied to the best achievable error within the class. Earlier general analyses included an extra factor, such as a disagreement coefficient, that restricted when they could establish an advantage.

Removing that factor from the leading term establishes a benefit for every concept class in the non-realizable case. The significance is specifically about the dominant theoretical cost of acquiring labels; the abstract does not equate it with a universal reduction in runtime or every finite-sample cost. Within that scope, the result resolves a longstanding question about the reach of agnostic active learning.
neurips-2025-agnostic-active-learning-is.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal agnostic active-learning query complexity and proves a strictly better leading term than passive learning for every concept class in the non-realizable case.

paragraphs: A generated image can look convincing while still failing to match its text description. This paper approaches that problem through the alignment of internal text and image representations. The authors argue that standard diffusion training on matching image-text pairs, using score-matching or flow-matching objectives, is suboptimal for this particular alignment goal.

Their proposed method, SoftREPA, adds contrastive fine-tuning to a pretrained model. It uses the existing dataset to supply both matching and nonmatching pairs, giving training a way to distinguish compatible representations from incompatible ones. Soft text tokens provide the adjustable representation mechanism, requiring fewer than one million additional trainable parameters and minimal computational overhead.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method explicitly increases mutual information between text and image representations, supporting stronger semantic consistency. Experiments on both text-to-image generation and text-guided editing report improved alignment. The contribution is a lightweight way to address representation mismatch using existing paired data, alongside approaches such as preference optimization that require specially prepared datasets.
neurips-2025-aligning-text-to-image-in-d.tldr: SoftREPA improves text-image semantic alignment through lightweight contrastive fine-tuning with soft text tokens and existing paired data.

paragraphs: People judge statements partly by considering why someone made them. A sales pitch, for example, comes with incentives that can affect its credibility. This paper studies whether language models show a comparable ability, called motivational vigilance: adjusting their interpretation of information according to a source's intentions and interests.

The authors first use controlled experiments drawn from cognitive science. In these settings, models discount biased testimony in a human-like way, and their behavior agrees with rational models of learning from motivated sources. The evaluation then moves to sponsored online advertisements, which more closely resemble information that language-model agents might encounter outside a controlled experiment.

In the advertising setting, model judgments follow the rational predictions much less closely. The authors attribute part of this gap to additional information that distracts models from relevant incentives. A simple intervention that makes intentions and incentives more salient substantially improves agreement. The findings support a basic sensitivity to communicative motives, while showing that this capacity does not transfer reliably to the more naturalistic setting tested.
neurips-2025-are-large-language-models-s.tldr: Language models discount motivated testimony in controlled tests but do so less reliably for online adverts, where highlighting incentives improves their judgments.

paragraphs: BevSplat estimates a ground camera's pose relative to a satellite image using noisy ground-truth annotations. These two views describe the same place from very different perspectives. A common strategy is to turn the ground image into a bird's-eye representation, creating a more comparable view for localization.

The difficulty is deciding how image content should be placed vertically when depth information and satellite height maps are unavailable. Earlier approaches either assume flat ground or use complex models to bridge the views. BevSplat represents each ground-image pixel as a three-dimensional Gaussian carrying semantic and spatial features. It then synthesizes these primitives into a bird's-eye feature map used for relative pose estimation.

This representation makes height-related spatial structure part of the process that connects ground and satellite views. The authors evaluate the method on KITTI and VIGOR, covering both pinhole-camera and panoramic query images. They report significantly improved localization accuracy over prior approaches. The findings support feature-based Gaussian primitives as an effective way to address height ambiguity in weakly supervised cross-view localization.
neurips-2025-bevsplat-resolving-height-a.tldr: BevSplat uses feature-bearing 3D Gaussians to address height ambiguity and improve camera localization against satellite imagery.

paragraphs: BioOSS explores a neural architecture inspired by activity that oscillates and spreads through biological neural circuits. The authors argue that standard perceptron-based architectures do not capture these dynamics, and that existing oscillatory systems still miss intricate interactions across space and time. Their focus is wave-like propagation, particularly as an inspiration drawn from the prefrontal cortex.

The system contains two interacting neuron populations. The p neurons are simplified units resembling membrane potentials, inspired by pyramidal cells in cortical columns. The o neurons control propagation velocities and modulate how activity spreads laterally. Local interactions between these populations generate wave-like activity patterns, while trainable damping and propagation-speed parameters let the dynamics adapt to a task.

The authors evaluate BioOSS on synthetic and real-world tasks and report better performance and interpretability than alternative architectures. The proposed value lies in making spatial propagation and temporal evolution explicit parts of computation. Its biological framing supplies the design inspiration; the stated empirical finding is that this architecture improves the tested learning tasks and makes its behavior more interpretable.
neurips-2025-biooss-a-bio-inspired-oscil.tldr: BioOSS uses interacting neuron populations with trainable wave dynamics, reporting improved task performance and interpretability.

paragraphs: A safety shield restricts which actions a reinforcement-learning system may take, using a model and formal safety analysis. Although this can enforce safety, the shield's own decisions can be difficult to understand. Representing the whole shield as one decision tree can become unwieldy because a shield may permit multiple actions in a given situation.

This paper organizes explanations into a hierarchy of decision trees. During design, a world model is used to assess the safety risks of actions in different states. That analysis produces both the shield and a high-level tree assigning states to safe, critical, dangerous, or unsafe categories. At runtime, smaller local trees explain which actions are allowed and why alternatives are considered unsafe.

The hierarchy separates understanding the current risk from understanding the available action choices. It uses information already required for shielding and is reported to add minimal overhead, making integration into existing pipelines straightforward. In experiments, the explanation trees are several orders of magnitude smaller than the original shield. The contribution makes the safety mechanism's decisions more accessible through localized, case-based explanations.
neurips-2025-explainably-safe-reinforcem.tldr: A hierarchy of compact decision trees explains the risk categories and action restrictions imposed by reinforcement-learning safety shields.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks are designed so that a transformation of the input produces a corresponding structured transformation internally. This paper extends that idea to transformations unfolding continuously over time, such as visual motion. These transformations are described as flows, mathematically represented by one-parameter Lie subgroups, and require attention to how a sequence evolves.

The authors first show that ordinary recurrent neural networks generally lack flow equivariance. When a stimulus moves, their hidden states need not change in a way that respects the geometry of that motion. They then show how to introduce flow equivariance into recurrent models, extending symmetry-aware network theory beyond static transformations and feed-forward architectures.

On next-step prediction and sequence classification, the proposed models significantly outperform non-equivariant counterparts in training speed and generalization to sequence lengths and velocities. These findings support encoding time-dependent symmetry directly in a sequence model. The work is presented as an initial step toward models whose internal dynamics respect continuous transformations in their inputs, with benefits demonstrated on the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-flow-equivariant-recurrent-.tldr: Flow-equivariant recurrent networks respect continuous transformations over time and improve training speed and length and velocity generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: FreshStack is a framework for automatically constructing retrieval benchmarks from technical documentation, code, and questions asked by communities. The aim is to test whether retrieval systems can find the information needed for challenging technical answers. Its evaluations focus on recent, fast-growing, and niche domains to create demanding retrieval tasks.

The construction process first collects a document corpus, then turns community questions and answers into smaller information units called nuggets. It identifies document support for those nuggets using a combination of retrieval methods and hybrid architectures. This creates a finer-grained basis for evaluation than considering only whether a retrieved document broadly concerns the question.

The authors build five datasets and find that out-of-the-box retrieval models substantially trail oracle approaches in every domain. Reranking fails to improve first-stage retrieval accuracy in two of the five domains, while oracle context helps a language model generate a high-quality retrieval-augmented answer. These findings reveal room to improve retrieval and show why stronger intermediate components do not automatically improve every domain. FreshStack is intended to support realistic, scalable benchmark construction.
neurips-2025-freshstack-building-realist.tldr: FreshStack builds technical retrieval benchmarks from community questions and documentation, revealing substantial performance gaps across five domains.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can influence one another in ways that involve entire groups, rather than only individual agents or pairs. Modeling these higher-order interactions can help explain how cooperation succeeds. The difficulty is that explicitly accounting for many combinations of agents can become prohibitively expensive, while opaque networks can hide the cooperation mechanisms they learn.

The paper introduces Continued Fraction Q-Learning, or QCoFr, as a value-decomposition framework. It can flexibly capture interactions of arbitrary order with complexity that grows linearly in the number of agents. The method also uses a variational information bottleneck to extract latent information for credit estimation, helping identify useful contributions while filtering noisy interactions.

The two components address complementary goals: representing rich cooperation efficiently and making the estimated contributions more informative. Experiments report consistently better performance and interpretability that agrees with the theoretical analysis. The central finding is that capturing high-order cooperation need not require combinatorial growth in this framework, and that filtering interaction information can improve both coordination and the understanding of agent contributions.
neurips-2025-high-order-interactions-mod.tldr: QCoFr models arbitrary-order agent interactions with linear complexity and filters noisy interaction information to improve cooperation and interpretability.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models the distribution of possible returns, giving it information beyond the average return used in classical formulations. This paper investigates why that richer prediction target can improve learning. Its starting point is a decomposition of the categorical distributional loss commonly used to train these models.

The decomposition reveals a distribution-matching entropy regularization term. According to the analysis, this term captures information about returns beyond their expectation and contributes an augmented reward signal during policy optimization. Its effect differs from ordinary maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, where the objective explicitly favors a diverse set of actions to encourage exploration.

Here, the derived regularization instead implicitly steers policy updates toward alignment with estimated environmental uncertainty. This provides an exploration-based explanation for the potential advantage of distributional learning. Extensive experiments support the importance of this uncertainty-aware regularization for the observed gains over classical reinforcement learning. The paper thus connects an existing training loss to a specific mechanism that may explain its empirical benefits, rather than asserting that distributional methods must always perform better.
neurips-2025-intrinsic-benefits-of-categ.tldr: Decomposing categorical distributional loss reveals uncertainty-aware regularization that helps explain distributional reinforcement learning's empirical advantages.

paragraphs: An image edit can appear visually plausible while failing to apply the knowledge required by an instruction. KRIS-Bench evaluates this distinction by testing knowledge-based reasoning in image-editing models. It treats editing as a task that can require factual understanding, conceptual relationships, or procedural knowledge, extending evaluation beyond the appearance of the output.

Drawing on educational theory, the benchmark organizes tasks into factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge categories. It includes 22 representative tasks across seven reasoning dimensions, with 1,267 annotated editing instances. This structure supports a diagnostic view of model capabilities: different tasks probe different kinds of knowledge instead of collapsing everything into a single notion of editing quality.

The authors also introduce an evaluation protocol featuring a Knowledge Plausibility metric, supported by knowledge hints and calibrated through human studies. Tests of nine state-of-the-art models reveal substantial reasoning gaps. The findings indicate that strong image generation and instruction following can coexist with weaknesses in knowledge-dependent editing, motivating evaluation that explicitly measures whether an edit makes sense given the knowledge it requires.
neurips-2025-kris-bench-benchmarking-nex.tldr: KRIS-Bench tests knowledge-based reasoning in image editing and finds substantial gaps across nine leading models.

paragraphs: Long videos produce large sequences of visual tokens, making video-language inference expensive as computation grows quadratically with sequence length. Selecting keyframes can reduce that burden, but selection itself can add work before feature encoding. It also makes a binary decision about each frame, even though different frames may warrant different amounts of retained detail.

DyToK uses attention already present in video-language models to guide compression without additional training. The authors find that attention layers encode query-dependent indications of which frames matter. DyToK turns these indications into different token-retention ratios for different frames, preserving more information from semantically rich frames and reducing redundant content elsewhere.

The method is compatible with existing compression techniques, including VisionZip and FastV. The abstract reports 2.5 times faster inference while preserving accuracy across multiple video-language models, including LLaVA-OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL. These results support allocating the token budget according to the question and frame content. The main contribution is a dynamic use of existing attention signals to improve the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff.
neurips-2025-less-is-more-but-where-dyna.tldr: DyToK uses existing attention signals to vary token retention across video frames, reporting 2.5× faster inference while preserving accuracy.

paragraphs: Training language models on detailed reasoning traces can improve reasoning, but those traces can also teach costly verbosity. This paper distinguishes the progressive steps that develop a solution from functional elements such as checking answers, trying alternatives, and correcting errors. Its aim is to reduce unnecessary functional material while retaining the complete core solution path.

Perplexity-based Importance Refinement, or PIR, scores reasoning steps according to their effect on confidence in the predicted answer. It selectively removes low-importance functional steps and preserves all progressive reasoning components. The resulting refined traces become training data, so the efficiency change is learned during fine-tuning and expressed in the model's later reasoning outputs.

Models trained on the refined data produce shorter reasoning chains while improving accuracy on AIME, AMC, and GPQA Diamond. The abstract reports accuracy gains of 0.9% to 6.6% and token reductions of 3% to 41%. Results across model sizes, data sources, and token budgets support the approach's generalizability within the tested settings. The findings show that selectively refining reasoning data can improve both inference efficiency and answer quality.
neurips-2025-limopro-reasoning-refinemen.tldr: PIR removes low-importance auxiliary reasoning from training traces, producing models that use fewer tokens and achieve higher accuracy on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion generates structured sequences through successive states, offering flexibility and control. The paper identifies a constraint in approaches that condition each step only on the current state: earlier generation history is unavailable, which can contribute to errors that cannot be corrected. This is the Markovian restriction that the proposed model removes.

CaDDi conditions on the full generative trajectory, allowing it to revisit and improve past states. A single non-Markovian transformer combines reasoning along the token sequence with reasoning across diffusion steps. The formulation includes standard causal language models as a special case and can directly reuse pretrained language-model weights without changing the architecture.

That compatibility provides a way to connect diffusion-style generation with the capabilities already learned by causal language models. On natural-language benchmarks, CaDDi outperforms state-of-the-art discrete diffusion baselines and substantially reduces the remaining gap to large autoregressive transformers. The results support using generation history as additional context, while the reported comparison indicates a narrowed gap rather than parity with autoregressive models.
neurips-2025-non-markovian-discrete-diff.tldr: CaDDi conditions discrete diffusion on the full generation history and reuses causal language-model weights to improve natural-language generation.

paragraphs: This paper provides theoretical guarantees for how quickly a Bayesian neural network's posterior concentrates around a true function as data accumulate. It studies anisotropic Besov spaces, which allow function regularity to differ across directions, and hierarchical compositions of such functions. These structures can have a lower intrinsic dimension than the full input dimension suggests.

The authors show that networks using either sparse priors or continuous shrinkage priors attain optimal posterior contraction rates for the studied function classes. The rates depend on the intrinsic dimension of the underlying structure, helping mitigate the curse of dimensionality. The priors also support adaptation: the optimal rate can be attained even when the true function's smoothness is unknown.

The framework includes additive and multiplicative Besov functions as special cases, covering multiple forms of structured dependence. Its contribution is a mathematical explanation of how Bayesian neural networks can exploit structure in high-dimensional estimation. The guarantee concerns the specified function classes and priors, linking statistical accuracy to intrinsic complexity and unknown smoothness rather than treating all high-dimensional functions as equally difficult.
neurips-2025-posterior-contraction-for-s.tldr: Sparse Bayesian neural networks achieve optimal, smoothness-adaptive posterior contraction rates governed by intrinsic dimension for the studied Besov function classes.

paragraphs: Safe-Sora embeds graphical watermarks directly into video generation to support copyright preservation of generated content. Its central observation is that watermarking performance depends strongly on visual similarity between a watermark and the content carrying it. The framework therefore makes placement part of the embedding process, using the video's own appearance to guide where watermark information goes.

A coarse-to-fine matching procedure divides the watermark image into patches. Each patch is assigned to a visually similar video frame and then localized to a suitable spatial region within that frame. To combine information across space and time, the method uses a Mamba architecture enhanced with a three-dimensional wavelet transform and a new scanning strategy.

This architecture models long-range dependencies during both watermark embedding and retrieval. Experiments report state-of-the-art results for video quality, watermark fidelity, and robustness, with the proposed components accounting for much of the improvement. The contribution combines content-adaptive placement with temporal modeling, addressing the need to preserve generated video quality while making the embedded graphical watermark recoverable.
neurips-2025-safe-sora-safe-text-to-vide.tldr: Safe-Sora embeds graphical watermarks during video generation using adaptive patch placement and a wavelet-enhanced Mamba architecture.

paragraphs: Local stochastic gradient descent is an important optimization method in decentralized federated learning. Knowing that its iterates converge does not by itself describe their statistical variability or provide tools for detecting unusual behavior. This paper develops Gaussian approximations that support statistical inference about both the final result and the learning process over time.

For the final local-SGD iterates, the authors prove a Berry-Esseen theorem, a result that controls the quality of a Gaussian approximation. This enables valid multiplier bootstrap procedures, using the approximation to justify statistical resampling. The work therefore extends the analysis beyond whether optimization approaches a solution to how its resulting uncertainty can be characterized.

The authors also introduce two distinct time-uniform Gaussian approximations for the entire trajectory. These support Gaussian bootstrap-based tests aimed at detecting adversarial attacks during learning. Extensive simulations support the theoretical results. The contribution connects distributional guarantees for decentralized optimization to practical statistical procedures, with separate tools for inference about final iterates and robustness-oriented assessment of the trajectory.
neurips-2025-sharp-gaussian-approximatio.tldr: Gaussian approximation results for local SGD justify bootstrap inference on final iterates and trajectory-based tests for adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions as a data-driven approach to solving partial differential equations. This paper argues that common computational domains can be poorly matched to the underlying PDE space. It proposes a Radon neural operator, or RNO, that transforms inputs into a sinogram representation to reduce the dimensionality of the transformations involved.

Within that representation, the authors find that different projection angles contribute unequally. They introduce angle reweighting to account for those differences, along with a convolutional layer operating on a fixed angular grid decoupled from the PDE space. The layer has a natural discrete-invariance guarantee, while the overall framework targets computation in an infinite-dimensional function space.

The theoretical analysis proves a bilipschitz strong-monotonicity property under diffeomorphism, providing a structural basis for the method's accuracy claims. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art scores across standard benchmarks and improved generalization. The contribution combines a different representation of the PDE problem with angle-aware computation and theoretical guarantees, rather than relying only on a more elaborate network operating in an existing transform domain.
neurips-2025-solving-partial-differentia.tldr: RNO uses Radon-transform representations and angle-aware computation to improve neural PDE solving, supported by theoretical properties and benchmark results.

paragraphs: The paper studies a principal and an agent who interact in a changing stochastic environment. Each observes information unavailable to the other, and both care about their total payoff across the full time horizon. The principal can commit to a policy for eliciting and signaling information; after communicating, the two players choose their actions independently.

Optimal behavior in this model requires policies that depend on interaction history. Explicitly storing all possible histories is infeasible because their number grows exponentially with model size. The authors address this through inducible value sets, shifting the algorithmic treatment toward achievable values rather than an explicit enumeration of every possible history.

These techniques yield an algorithm that computes an approximately optimal principal policy in time polynomial in the inverse accuracy tolerance. The authors also handle unknown transition probabilities in an episodic reinforcement-learning setting. Their learning algorithm achieves regret of order T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors, for both players over T episodes. This sublinear growth means average regret decreases as interaction continues, while retaining history-dependent decision making.
neurips-2025-stochastic-principal-agent-.tldr: Inducible value sets enable efficient approximate history-dependent policies and sublinear-regret learning in a stochastic principal-agent model.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a large teacher model into a smaller student. This paper identifies a security threat in which a backdoor remains dormant in the teacher but becomes active in the student through distillation. The activation can occur even when the distillation dataset is clean, making the transfer process itself central to the vulnerability.

The proposed method, SCAR, frames this as a bilevel optimization problem. An inner optimization simulates distillation by training a surrogate student. An outer optimization uses that student's outputs to modify the teacher so that the unwanted behavior emerges after transfer. The method handles the nested optimization through implicit differentiation and a pre-optimized trigger injection function.

Experiments across datasets, model architectures, and distillation techniques support the attack's effectiveness and resistance to existing backdoor detection. The finding is that examining a teacher for directly observable backdoor behavior can miss behavior expressed by its distilled students. It exposes a conditional vulnerability in model compression: a teacher's apparent behavior before transfer may not reveal the security properties of the model learned from it.
neurips-2025-taught-well-learned-ill-tow.tldr: SCAR demonstrates backdoors that remain dormant in teacher models but activate in distilled students, even with clean distillation data.

paragraphs: Different foundation models can learn similar representations despite differences in architecture, objectives, and modality. This paper proposes that the convergence reflects a shared relational structure: samples acquire meaning partly through their relationships to other samples. The Indra Representation Hypothesis develops this view beyond treating each sample's internal representation as an independent abstraction.

The authors formalize a sample's representation as its relational profile with respect to other samples, using the V-enriched Yoneda embedding from category theory. Under a given cost function, they show that this formulation is unique, complete, and structure-preserving. Those mathematical properties apply to the specified formulation; the broader claim about what foundation models converge toward is presented as a hypothesis.

For practical evaluation, the authors instantiate the relational representation with angular distance. Experiments involving vision, language, and audio report consistent improvements in robustness and alignment across architectures and modalities. The resulting approach aligns unimodal foundation models without training. Its contribution connects a relational explanation of representational convergence to a concrete transformation that improves cross-model and cross-modal alignment in the tested settings.
neurips-2025-the-indra-representation-hy.tldr: Indra represents samples through their relationships to others, providing a theoretically grounded, training-free approach that improves multimodal alignment in experiments.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models can be powerful but difficult to deploy with limited computing resources. This paper introduces Unified Reinforcement and Imitation Learning, or RIL, to train smaller models with stronger generative abilities. The approach combines learning from large teachers with reinforcement signals that help the student improve its own outputs.

The imitation component is adversarial: a language-model-based discriminator learns to distinguish student outputs from teacher outputs. This gives the student feedback connected to how its text generation differs from that of larger models. Multiple teacher vision-language models provide diverse guidance, while reinforcement learning adds another source of improvement within the same training strategy.

Experiments across vision-language benchmarks report significant performance gains and a narrower gap to leading open- and closed-source models. The students are competitive with leading closed-source systems and surpass state-of-the-art models in several evaluated instances. The findings support combining reinforcement and imitation as an efficient route to stronger lightweight models, with the reported successes depending on the benchmark instances rather than establishing superiority across all tasks.
neurips-2025-unified-reinforcement-and-i.tldr: RIL combines reinforcement learning with adversarial imitation from multiple teachers to train lightweight vision-language models with stronger benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Learning a skill from video is difficult for an autonomous agent because the footage supplies visual observations without action labels or rewards. BCV-LR addresses this by learning latent representations of actions, then connecting those representations to actions the agent can actually execute. The goal is to learn useful behavior with few environment interactions.

The framework first uses self-supervised tasks to extract action-related features from video. A dynamics-based unsupervised objective then predicts latent actions between consecutive frames. Online interactions align these pretrained latent actions with the real action space, enabling behavior cloning. The cloned policy collects additional experience, which supports further latent-action refinement and another round of policy improvement.

Across challenging discrete- and continuous-control tasks, the method achieves effective policies with few interactions, reaching expert-level performance on some tasks. It surpasses imitation-from-video baselines and reward-equipped reinforcement-learning methods in sample efficiency on 24 of 28 tasks. The result supports videos as a strong source of supervision without other expert annotations, while the learning process still uses online interaction to connect inferred actions to executable behavior.
neurips-2025-videos-are-sample-efficient.tldr: BCV-LR learns latent actions from videos and aligns them through limited interaction, improving sample efficiency over comparison methods on 24 of 28 tasks.
